nicheStories.title: Iran and Ukraine depleted 'virtually all' US long-range missiles: Report
nicheStories.description: Reuters reported this morning that the U.S. has used “virtually all” its long-range precision strike missiles during its war on Iran.Reuters’ sources would not say exactly how many of these surface to surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), the U.S. military has left.This comes amid news that the U.S. has burned through other key weapons systems since war with Iran began. Last week, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated the U.S. has fewer than 827 Patriot missiles, and fewer than 278 THAAD ballistic missile interceptors, in its stockpiles.But the depletion began long ago with the Ukraine war. Since 2022, the U.S. gave  weapons to Kyiv at rates faster than it could replace them, including Patriot missile interceptors and an unspecified number of ATACMS.Despite the growing body of evidence, President Donald Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and UN Ambassador Mike Waltz have repeatedly denied the U.S. is running low on critical munitions. Not surprisingly, the U.S. has taken great strides to procure munitions in recent months, including repeatedly floating major spending packages to replenish depleted stockpiles. The latest: a $18.2 billion request for more money for the Pentagon budget.Earlier this spring, the Pentagon awarded RTX a $441 million contract for PAC-2 missiles — older Patriot missiles, which the U.S. has not ordered in decades. The Pentagon has also asked civilian companies, such as Ford, GM, and Oshkosh, to consider making weapons.Last month, a U.S. official told the Washington Post that there weren't enough munitions to sustain military operations in the Middle East. "I don't think the White House is aware of that,” the official said. Munitions are expensive and often take years to build.

nicheStories.title: US is the real loser if Senate passes virtue signaling Russia sanctions
nicheStories.description: As the Senate returns to Washington for its last week in session until mid-September, it faces a long to-do list. But for many senators, the top priority is not enacting legislation that will help Americans but instead rushing to approve the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, known colloquially as the “Russia sanctions bill.”A passion project of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill is intended to increase economic pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin. The legislation’s backers hope that, by choking off funding for Russia’s war effort, they can force Moscow to make greater concessions in ongoing negotiations to end the four-year old conflict in Ukraine. But this logic and the bill itself are fundamentally flawed. The new legislation will have a limited effect on Russia’s fortunes; as has been the case since the beginning of the war, additional economic punishments are unlikely to be decisive in Putin’s calculus. In fact, the bill is more likely to harden the Russian position than to soften it. The bill contains three main types of provisions. First, it codifies and expands sanctions against Kremlin officials, Russian oligarchs, and Russian banks and corporations. Second, it cracks down on Russia’s shadow fleet, increasing penalties against tankers and companies accused of trying to smuggle oil or evade the Western price cap on Russian oil sales. Third and most significantly, it grants the president the authority to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, though it exempts allies who are reducing their purchases from Russia over time. The bill also allows the president to waive required penalties if deemed important for U.S. national security. To be sure, if the new bill is passed by Congress and implemented by the White House, it will be economically painful for Russia. The sanctions it prescribes would fully sever Russian banks and energy corporations from the SWIFT system, including Gazprombank, which handles energy transactions. The bill also threatens secondary sanctions and loss of access to SWIFT for third-party intermediaries that continue to process payments from or interact with sanctioned entities. Combined with the bill’s measures aimed at Russia’s shadow fleet, these new sanctions will further complicate any Russian efforts to export oil.However, after more than four years of sanctions, Russian banks and corporations have already developed alternatives. For example, they can turn to small regional banks that have little exposure to U.S. markets. They can also rely on layered shell companies that work through friendly countries, transactions conducted through “stablecoin” digital currencies, and even direct country-to-country bartering in which Russian commodities are swapped for machinery, microelectronics, or other goods. None of these approaches is convenient, but they will allow Russia to weather even the more draconian penalties included in the new bill.The bill’s tariff provisions are likely to have even less effect on Russia’s revenues. Theoretically, the legislation targets the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas, a list that would include key U.S. allies like France, Japan, Spain, Turkey, and Belgium. But members of Congress, fearful of giving Trump more authority to use tariffs punitively against U.S. allies, included a waiver for countries that account for less than 15% of Russian exports and are working to decrease their dependency on Russia over time. This list applies to just about every country that might be hit with tariffs for continuing to buy Russian oil and gas, except for three: China, India, and Hungary.Even if Trump chooses to apply tariffs to these countries, the consequences may be worse for the United States than for Russia. Tariffs on India could cause Russia real economic pain, as New Delhi has shown itself to be sensitive to threats of U.S. economic penalty. But if the conflict in Iran continues to snarl oil markets, India will face constraints on its ability to shift its demand for oil elsewhere. Moreover, the United States has already tried sanctions on India as a way to pressure Russia, and it didn’t work. It did, however, damage U.S. ties with an important partner in Asia.China is the leading buyer of both Russian natural gas and oil, and likely the primary target of the bill’s writers. But using tariffs to penalize Chinese oil purchases would be suicidal for Trump. He’s already run the experiment of putting 100% tariffs on Chinese goods, back on Liberation Day in April 2025. The result was so bad for the U.S. economy that it led to the original Trump TACO (Trump Always Chickens Out). Since then, China has shown its willingness to use its dominance in rare earth minerals to retaliate against what it sees as unfair U.S. trade practices, and it would likely do so again if Trump levies tariffs under the authority of the new legislation. But even smaller tariffs on China are unlikely, since Trump is unlikely to do anything in the near term that derails his September meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.In the end, the new legislation is unlikely to be the knockout blow that forces Putin to give up on his core demands. The tariff provision may affect Russian oil and gas income on the margins, but its effect will be limited by the Trump administration’s higher priority political goals. Russia’s economy is under strain, but it can withstand the modest costs that Graham’s sanctions bill will impose while sustaining the war effort.More importantly, the legislation’s underlying premise — that increased economic pressure is the key to ending the war in Ukraine — is as incorrect today as it was back in 2022. Putin has made clear time and again that he is willing to pay a very high price to achieve what he considers to be an acceptable outcome in Ukraine. He views the war as existential, for Russia and for himself personally, and has been largely insensitive to economic levers since the conflict began. This is unlikely to change.In fact, the new legislation is much more likely to strengthen Russia’s resolve and work against peace. It may do this in two ways. First, it fuels Putin’s narrative that the conflict in Ukraine is really a war between Russia and the West, a storyline that can shore up domestic support and that increases the risks that the war eventually widens. Second, it confirms for Moscow that the United States is not actually interested in peace or in serving as a mediator but rather continues to harbor Biden administration-era hopes of weakening Russia over the long-term. Many in the U.S. Congress probably realize this but will vote for the bill anyway, a virtue signaling gesture taken at the expense of the voters who elected them. In fact, if there is a loser from this legislation it will be the United States, which will face economic uncertainty and the loss of geopolitical influence as more countries tire of the United States using the dollar as a weapon and look for alternatives.

nicheStories.title: Robert Kagan: Sometimes US intervention is worth blowback
nicheStories.description: Robert Kagan surprised some people. One of America’s most influential hawks condemned the Trump administration’s botched war in Iran, suggesting in The Atlantic in March that U.S. involvement in the Middle East has been a catalyst of, rather than a prudent response to, Islamic terrorism.A senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and prolific historian, Kagan has advocated U.S. primacy for decades, starting with his support for Nicaragua’s Contra insurgents as the head of the State Department’s Office of Public Diplomacy (1985-88). In 1997, Kagan co-founded Project for the New American Century, a neoconservative think tank that lobbied for a muscular foreign policy and the maintenance of U.S. global hegemony. The group exercised its considerable influence to push regime change in Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. Kagan’s advocacy has always been based on a belief that the world would collapse into disorder without American leadership, even though U.S. military misadventures have repeatedly destabilized parts of the world. So, is Robert Kagan now reconsidering his past hawkishness? I interviewed him to find out. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.Martin Di Caro: Are you undergoing a conversion? Is that fair?Robert Kagan: I don't think so, because I never denied that blowback was a reality. In fact, my writing shows that when the United States is out there acting in the world, Americans tend to not even be aware of the effect of American power on other nations. And so they're constantly shocked whenever the use of American power leads to a response. The best example is Japan and Pearl Harbor. Many Americans acted like it was out of the blue when Japan attacked us when, in fact, the U.S. pursued policies that were likely to lead to a Japanese attack. The same was true of 9/11 in the sense that it was at least in part a response to the American presence in the Middle East. The question is, do you act even though you know that there is going to be blowback because the stakes are worth it. So, I never doubted it and, as I say, recognizing the effect of American power on other nations is an important part of my history.Di Caro: Yet for decades you have advocated for U.S. interventionism and, in the case of the Iraq invasion of 2003, a preemptive war…Kagan: Wait a minute. Can we stop right there? When you say that I’ve advocated for intervention for decades, what in particular are you talking about? I certainly supported the interventions in Bosnia and Kosovo, but it's not like I was just calling for intervention everywhere at all times. That's a shorthand that you use, but it's what people think, you know?Di Caro: Well, you've never called for an invasion of Iran, but you did support the Contras when you were a member of Reagan's State Department going back to the 1980s.Kagan: Totally. Right. Di Caro: So that's what I'm referring to.Kagan: I definitely believe in the exercise of U.S. power in the world. Sometimes that means intervention, but frequently it doesn't necessarily mean intervention.Di Caro: Do you reject the neoconservative label?Kagan: I do reject it, not only because it has taken on connotations that I think are frankly antisemitic, but because it's just a bad description of what I am. What I am is a liberal. Lib-er-al. My foreign policy is liberal. If you look back on the history of American foreign policy, the people who have pursued the policies that I favor have always tended to be progressive and liberal. And conservative foreign policy in America has always tended to be in the direction of restraint. I worked for the neoconservatives. I worked for Irving Kristol. They were called neoconservatives because they had been on the left and then they were newly on the right. I have never accepted it as a reasonable definition [of my views].Di Caro: We can set aside definitional debates because it may be more important to talk about the consequences of the policies that you've advocated, however you’re labeled, because you're not just some blogger. You’ve been an influential voice in foreign policy. Given your recent commentary about Iran, have you reconsidered your past support for U.S. wars, namely the invasion of Iraq in 2003?Kagan: I went through the process of thinking about my support for the Iraq war long before this Iran issue came up. Look, the key thing about Iraq then and Iran now is the circumstances are just totally different than in 2003. That's not to say that, in retrospect, [the Iraq war] did not turn out to be a mistake, but the strategic arguments were completely different than they are now, and the overall aim of American foreign policy at that time was entirely different from the overall aim of foreign policy now.The strategic context mattered. In 2003 we were not concerned about rising great power challenges. Russia was essentially still on its back. The Chinese were in their Hu Jintao-Wen Jiabao mode. There was no particular threat to the world order when the United States went to war in Iraq. To answer your question, I haven't really fundamentally changed my mind. These are different circumstances. You'd have to assume that I had some kind of doctrine of always invading the Middle East whenever possible. But that has not been my doctrine.Di Caro: In 2003 I thought invading Iraq was justified. I'm ashamed that I had such poor judgment. The Iraq war was unnecessary. Kagan: You say it was unnecessary because you don't take seriously the nature of the threat that was posed.Di Caro: What threat did Saddam Hussein pose? He was a tinpot dictator with a hollowed-out military.Kagan: I don't agree with you. He was not just a tinpot dictator. He was actually special. He had already committed two major acts of aggression against his neighbors. By the way, that’s something that Iran has never done. Saddam had invaded Iran. He had invaded Kuwait. He clearly wanted to be the Saladin of the Middle East. You can feel however you want about it, but you were not alone in supporting the Iraq war. It's bizarre to look back and think that it was somehow a peculiar judgment that Saddam posed a threat, when almost everybody including the Clinton administration thought Saddam was a threat. It was practically a consensus view.When the war went bad, a lot of people wanted to pretend that they never supported it and decided that it was an incredibly stupid thing to do. I just don't think it's right to go back and say this was a silly activity when such a significant majority of Americans, including members of Congress, thought that it was an important thing to do.Di Caro: But we can see how disastrous the consequences were. According to The Costs of War Project at Brown University, there were at least 180,000 civilian deaths from direct war violence, and it was the U.S. invasion that triggered all the chaos and the civil war that ensued. 4,500 U.S. service members and 3,600 American contractors were killed…Kagan: In ten years! Over ten years. Di Caro: …millions of people were displaced across the Middle East in the post-9/11 wars. Trillions of dollars for the U.S. Treasury when we factor in decades of long-term care for our veterans. I'm having trouble understanding why you can't admit that this was a mistake.Kagan: Well, I didn't say I can't admit that it was a mistake. I'm not sure what the utility of admitting that it was a mistake is. It's not going to bring anybody back to life. But, you know, there were obviously elements of the Iraq war that were a mistake. I was very clear about it at the time when it was obvious that the administration not only hadn't sent in enough troops initially, but also didn't understand the role that those troops had to play because [Donald] Rumsfeld, from the moment that they invaded, wanted to get out. And so we didn't accept the responsibility that, as Colin Powell said, when you break it, you own it.The biggest effect that I regret is how it influenced Americans’ attitudes towards foreign policy in general… In retrospect it is clear that Americans had become increasingly unenthusiastic about the role the United States was playing in the world.Di Caro: There were good reasons for Americans souring on what I call military misadventures. There’s the harm done to other peoples, but also the returns for the United States have been meager.Kagan: That's what you say, but your whole line of discussion takes for granted all the ways in which the overall American approach to the world produced enormous benefits both for much of the world and for the United States. You take for granted the world order that was in existence. And I'll tell you what, we're not going to be able to take it for granted anymore because we are now experimenting with the world that, I guess, you think would’ve been better, a world in which the United States is basically staying at home and minding its own business.Di Caro: That's not true. My position is that the United States has other tools rather than the almost exclusive application of hard power and coercion. Kagan: You think we didn't use any of the other tools as well? I think we wound up using military force because the other tools weren't working.Di Caro: Soft power. This is something the political scientist Robert Keohane has discussed… Kagan: You’re going to teach me about soft power now?Di Caro: No, but don’t you agree the U.S. has neglected soft power recently?Kagan: I do not. I do not. And there’s a whole myth about the Iraq war that it somehow led to the disenchantment of the rest of the world with the United States and, therefore, we suffered a reputational disaster. In fact, the U.S. alliances, including countries that opposed the Iraq war, were not only strong but actually strengthened in the second half of [George W.] Bush’s presidency. If your view is that the United States has undermined its position in the world, then why do all the allies continue to rely on the United States for their protection, even though it's allegedly this ogre? There's just no logic to that. As the Trump administration destroys the U.S. position, the rest of the world is basically in mourning for a United States that used to be. Di Caro: Do you think the GCC states still want American bases within their boundaries? Kagan: Not now, but not because of the Iraq war. It’s because the United States has proved [under Trump] to be a terribly unreliable ally. Not because they think the United States is immoral. Do you think they're worried about American morality? What they’re upset about is that the United States proved to be an inadequate protector. If Iran had not been able to hit them with all the drones and the missiles, I don't think they would have turned against the United States. They were largely supportive of getting rid of the regime in Iran. It's just that the United States both failed to do that and was unable to protect them.Another reason that I thought this was a bad idea, which is not about changing doctrines, is that the one thing we learned in the 1990s was that you cannot bomb your way to success in these situations. When they went after Slobodan Milošević [in Yugoslavia], I remember getting a briefing from [General] Wesley Clark, who said after four days of bombing, Milošević is going to cave. And 90 days later, it required the threat of an American ground force to get him to retire. So I think we knew that you couldn’t get rid of [Iran’s] nuclear program and certainly not get regime change simply by bombing people.My problem with some of the critics of American policy is that they don't care what happens when America is not involved. They're only interested when America is involved. So when Saddam Hussein, for instance, was killing 200,000 Kurds and other minorities in Iraq using chemical weapons, nobody cared about those 200,000. They only care about the lives that are lost as a consequence of American action. There's quite a double standard in judging American behavior… Di Caro: You mentioned Saddam and the Kurds. That double standard also applies to the U.S. government. Kagan: Yes, I know. We also abandoned the Kurds. Di Caro: The United States looked the other way in the 1980s when Saddam gassed the Kurds, and right up until the eve of the invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, George H.W. Bush was sending Saddam Hussein chummy letters telling him how much he wanted to nurture their relationship. It was only after the invasion of Kuwait when Saddam Hussein became Adolf Hitler.Kagan: I agree. Do you want to make the case that the United States is a deeply flawed country that does the wrong thing sometimes? Because if you do, I'm perfectly in agreement with that.Di Caro: My point is that the Gulf War was a Pyrrhic victory. The United States has never been able to extract itself from the Middle East.Some would argue Israel is one reason why the United States can't seem to extract itself, at least from the conflict with Iran.Kagan: Well, that's certainly been true.Di Caro: Why have recent U.S. administrations utterly failed to restrain Israel despite the fact that the U.S. has considerable leverage?Kagan: There are multiple elements to the answer. One is obviously the role of Jews in influencing American policy, which is a reality just the way the Irish, Italians, or Greeks have influenced American policy. The other thing is America is broadly Islamophobic, and so any enemy of Islam is a friend of ours for many Americans. I think Islamophobia is a reality in the United States, and Israel is supposed to be the bulwark against Islam.That's unfortunate. My view is that we should not have a foreign policy based on Islamophobia. We should be able to have perfectly good relations with Islamic countries and with Islam itself.Di Caro: What's your view of Israel's conduct in Gaza? How can we talk about a “rules-based order” after the world allowed that to happen? Israel’s conduct was enabled by the United States.Kagan: I myself almost never talk about a rules-based order because the United States has definitely pursued a double standard with regard to the rules-based order. You could say that we supported the rules-based order in the breach as much as in the observance.Di Caro: You sound like a restrainer now.Kagan: Well, this is the thing again. It’s like if you acknowledge that America does bad things in the world, then that makes you a “restrainer.” In my view, it just makes you analytically honest. Knowing that the United States does bad things does not answer the question of should the United States be involved in the world. Di Caro: The question is how the U.S. should be involved in the world.Kagan: Critiques of the American order are legitimate. The question is what is a better alternative? If you want to tell me let's never get involved in the Middle East again, I would say sure. I'm delighted to never get involved in the Middle East again. But that is not what the restrainers are fundamentally talking about. They're talking about getting out of the whole alliance structure system and ending the nature of American leadership since 1945. The assumption behind that has to be that the world is going to be at least as calm or calmer, and there'll be less turmoil. And I just absolutely reject that. I think there is going to be more turmoil. And I think there are a lot of things that the restrainers are not thinking about and they're almost in my view a little utopian in their assumption that a multipolar world can exist in some kind of peaceful harmony when I think history suggests otherwise.
